points: Feed pressure was held at 15 bar and feed temperature at 25 degrees Celsius throughout the run.
Permeate flux at the start was 42 litres per square metre per hour.
Permeate flux after 120 hours of operation was 38 litres per square metre per hour, a decline of 9.5 percent from the start value.
Salt rejection was 98.2 percent at the start and 97.9 percent at the end of the run.
Calcium concentration in the feed was 1.8 millimoles per litre.
Chemical cleaning restored permeate flux to 41 litres per square metre per hour.
definitions: reverse osmosis = a separation process in which pressure drives water through a dense membrane that retains dissolved salts
permeate flux = the volume of water passing through unit membrane area per unit time
salt rejection = the fraction of feed salt concentration retained by the membrane, stated as a percentage
limits: The decline applies to the stated feed composition and pressure only.
Cleaning recovery was measured on the same membrane element after the run.
prose: Reverse osmosis is a separation process in which pressure drives water through a dense membrane that retains dissolved salts. Permeate flux is the volume of water passing through unit membrane area per unit time, and permeate flux is the quantity tracked through the run. Feed pressure was held at 15 bar and feed temperature at 25 degrees Celsius throughout the run. Permeate flux at the start was 42 litres per square metre per hour. The membrane element received feed at constant composition, and the element operated without interruption between samples. Permeate flux after 120 hours of operation was 38 litres per square metre per hour, a decline of 9.5 percent from the start value. The decline developed gradually, with the steepest change in the early part of the run and a slower change near the end. A flux decline at constant pressure and constant temperature points to added resistance at the membrane surface, and the resistance grew while bulk feed conditions stayed fixed. Salt rejection is the fraction of feed salt concentration retained by the membrane, stated as a percentage. Salt rejection was 98.2 percent at the start and 97.9 percent at the end of the run. Calcium concentration in the feed was 1.8 millimoles per litre, and calcium is the cation most closely linked to scale formation on this feed. The small change in salt rejection against the larger change in flux separates a surface deposit from membrane damage, because a damaged membrane passes more salt as flux falls. Chemical cleaning restored permeate flux to 41 litres per square metre per hour. Recovery near the start value after cleaning supports a removable deposit as the cause of the decline, and the deposit accounts for the added resistance during the run. The decline applies to the stated feed composition and pressure only, and a feed with a different calcium load may show a different rate of decline. Cleaning recovery was measured on the same membrane element after the run, and recovery on a fresh element may differ.

points: The digester operated at a hydraulic retention time of 20 days and an organic loading rate of 2.5 kilograms of chemical oxygen demand per cubic metre per day.
Biogas yield was 0.62 cubic metres per kilogram of volatile solids fed.
The control digester, fed the same substrate without the test additive, gave a biogas yield of 0.51 cubic metres per kilogram of volatile solids fed.
Methane content of the biogas was 64 percent by volume.
Volatile solids reduction across the digester was 58 percent.
Digester temperature was held at 37 degrees Celsius and the trial ran for 90 days.
Mean digester pH was 7.2.
Ammonia nitrogen concentration in the digester liquor was 1.4 grams per litre at the end of the trial.
definitions: anaerobic digestion = a biological process in which microorganisms convert organic matter to biogas in the absence of oxygen
chemical oxygen demand = the oxygen equivalent of the organic matter in a feed, measured by chemical oxidation
volatile solids = the fraction of solids lost on ignition, used as a measure of organic content
hydraulic retention time = the mean time feed spends in the digester, from digester volume divided by feed flow
pH = a measure of acidity on a logarithmic scale
limits: The yield advantage over the control applies at the stated loading rate and temperature.
Ammonia inhibition sets the upper bound for nitrogen-rich feeds under the same conditions.
prose: Anaerobic digestion is a biological process in which microorganisms convert organic matter to biogas in the absence of oxygen. Chemical oxygen demand is the oxygen equivalent of the organic matter in a feed, measured by chemical oxidation, and chemical oxygen demand sets the loading basis for the trial. Volatile solids are the fraction of solids lost on ignition, and volatile solids serve as the yield basis. Hydraulic retention time is the mean time feed spends in the digester, from digester volume divided by feed flow. The digester operated at a hydraulic retention time of 20 days and an organic loading rate of 2.5 kilograms of chemical oxygen demand per cubic metre per day. Biogas yield was 0.62 cubic metres per kilogram of volatile solids fed. The control digester, fed the same substrate without the test additive, gave a biogas yield of 0.51 cubic metres per kilogram of volatile solids fed. The yield difference between the digesters appeared after the additive reached a steady dose, and the difference persisted across the sampling rounds that followed. Methane content of the biogas was 64 percent by volume. A higher methane content at a higher yield indicates conversion of a larger share of the fed organic matter, with no sign of dilution of the biogas by other gases. Volatile solids reduction across the digester was 58 percent. Volatile solids reduction and biogas yield move together in this trial, and the pair gives a consistent picture of organic matter destruction in the digester. Digester temperature was held at 37 degrees Celsius and the trial ran for 90 days. pH, a measure of acidity on a logarithmic scale, had a mean value of 7.2 in the digester. Ammonia nitrogen concentration in the digester liquor was 1.4 grams per litre at the end of the trial. Ammonia nitrogen rose slowly during the trial, and the final concentration stayed below the range linked to inhibition in comparable digesters. The yield advantage over the control applies at the stated loading rate and temperature, and ammonia inhibition sets the upper bound for nitrogen-rich feeds under the same conditions.

points: Inlet air temperature was 180 degrees Celsius and outlet air temperature was 85 degrees Celsius.
Feed solids content was 45 percent by mass.
Product moisture in the earlier run at an outlet air temperature of 78 degrees Celsius was 4.8 percent by mass.
Product moisture at the stated conditions was 3.2 percent by mass.
Feed rate was 250 kilograms per hour.
Atomiser speed was 18000 revolutions per minute.
Powder recovery in the cyclone and bag filter was 96 percent of the fed solids.
definitions: spray drying = a process in which a liquid feed is atomised into a hot gas stream and dried to a powder
product moisture = the mass of water per unit mass of wet product, stated as a percentage
atomiser = a rotating wheel that breaks the feed into droplets
limits: Product moisture applies to the stated feed solids content and outlet air temperature.
prose: Spray drying is a process in which a liquid feed is atomised into a hot gas stream and dried to a powder. Product moisture is the mass of water per unit mass of wet product, stated as a percentage, and product moisture is the quality variable for the run. Inlet air temperature was 180 degrees Celsius and outlet air temperature was 85 degrees Celsius. Outlet air temperature is set by the balance between evaporation load and air flow, and outlet air temperature is the control handle for product moisture in this dryer. Feed solids content was 45 percent by mass. A higher feed solids content lowers the evaporation load per unit of powder, and feed solids content was held steady by the feed preparation step. Product moisture in the earlier run at an outlet air temperature of 78 degrees Celsius was 4.8 percent by mass. Product moisture at the stated conditions was 3.2 percent by mass. The moisture fall between the runs tracks the rise in outlet air temperature, and the tracking matches the drying behaviour expected from the evaporation balance. Feed rate was 250 kilograms per hour. Feed rate fixes the evaporation load at a given feed solids content, and feed rate was logged at each sampling point. The atomiser is a rotating wheel that breaks the feed into droplets, and droplet size sets the drying time for each particle. Atomiser speed was 18000 revolutions per minute. Droplet size stayed in the intended range at the stated atomiser speed, and no coarse fraction appeared in the product samples. Powder recovery in the cyclone and bag filter was 96 percent of the fed solids. Powder recovery at this level leaves a small loss to the exhaust, and the loss fraction was stable across the run. Product moisture at the stated conditions applies to the stated feed solids content and outlet air temperature, and a feed with a different solids content needs a new outlet temperature setting.

points: Corrosion rate of the unprotected steel in aerated seawater was 0.84 millimetres per year.
Corrosion rate of the same steel in deaerated seawater was 0.12 millimetres per year.
Exposure lasted 180 days.
Chloride concentration in the seawater was 0.6 moles per litre.
Seawater temperature was 30 degrees Celsius.
The inhibitor treatment reduced the corrosion rate in aerated seawater to 0.21 millimetres per year.
Maximum pit depth on the unprotected coupons was 0.45 millimetres.
definitions: corrosion rate = the thickness loss of a metal per unit time
coupon = a small specimen of the metal exposed to the environment for a measured period
pitting = localised attack that forms cavities in the surface
limits: The rates apply to the stated chloride concentration and temperature.
Pit depth was measured on the coupon set from this exposure.
prose: Corrosion rate is the thickness loss of a metal per unit time, and corrosion rate is the comparison basis for the exposures. A coupon is a small specimen of the metal exposed to the environment for a measured period, and mass loss on each coupon gives the corrosion rate for that exposure. Coupon surfaces were cleaned of corrosion product before weighing, and cleaning followed the same procedure for every coupon in the set. Corrosion rate of the unprotected steel in aerated seawater was 0.84 millimetres per year. Corrosion rate of the same steel in deaerated seawater was 0.12 millimetres per year. The contrast between the exposures assigns the larger share of the attack to dissolved oxygen, and oxygen reduction is the cathodic reaction that supports the higher rate. Exposure lasted 180 days. Chloride concentration in the seawater was 0.6 moles per litre. Chloride acts on the surface film that limits attack on steel, and film breakdown under chloride exposure opens the surface to pitting. Seawater temperature was 30 degrees Celsius. Temperature raises the rate of the surface reactions, and the stated temperature matches the service condition for the comparison. The inhibitor treatment reduced the corrosion rate in aerated seawater to 0.21 millimetres per year. The inhibitor forms an adsorbed layer on the steel surface, and the layer lowers the area available for the corrosion reactions. Pitting is localised attack that forms cavities in the surface, and pitting governs the service limit for thin sections. Maximum pit depth on the unprotected coupons was 0.45 millimetres. Pit depth exceeds the mean thickness loss on the same coupons, and pit depth sets the perforation risk for a pipe wall at the stated corrosion rate. The rates apply to the stated chloride concentration and temperature, and a seawater with a different chloride load may give different rates. Pit depth was measured on the coupon set from this exposure, and pit depth on longer exposures may grow beyond the stated value.
